exp.2:12:
He says God went out to rescue his people, together with his anointed one, that is, the king chosen by Him (some think this refers to the king of Israel, others to the Messiah). It speaks of tearing down the family or power of the wicked, like a building that has its foundations stripped away until it lies in ruins. "Selah" is a pause for reflection.

Habakkuk, the prophet, is praying with a song. He remembers the great works of God in the past, such as the Exodus, to encourage himself while he waits for judgment on Judah and on the oppressors. He describes God as a warrior who defends his own.

For today: when evil seems stronger than you, remember what God has already done for his people. Place your trust in the fact that He knows how to save and to bring down injustice in his time. Take a pause today and thank him for one time he helped you.
exp.0:7:
It says that the army of the Chaldeans will be extremely swift and fierce. Their horses run faster than leopards (in the older version, "tigers") and are fiercer than hungry wolves at evening. Their horsemen are many and come from distant lands, and they rush down like eagles swooping suddenly on their prey. The word "fierce" here means fierce or ravenous.

God speaks here, answering Habakkuk's complaint about the violence and injustice in Judah. God tells him that He will use the Chaldeans, or Babylonians, as an instrument of judgment. Habakkuk is alarmed, because that people is cruel. Later, the prophet will keep asking questions, and God will answer him.

For today: even when it seems that evil advances without restraint, God continues to govern history. You can bring Him your questions with honesty, as Habakkuk did, and trust that He acts with justice, even when you do not yet understand.
exp.2:6:
Habakkuk says that he saw the tents of Cushan full of distress, and that the land of Midian trembled. "Tents" refers to the camps or dwellings of those peoples. The word "distress" means fear and suffering. They trembled when they saw that God was drawing near.

Habakkuk prays and remembers the great works of God in the past, when He saved His people. Cushan is mentioned only here, and it is not known with certainty who they were: some think it was a people near Midian, or that both names refer to the same region. What is clear is that the nations trembled before God. Habakkuk recalls this to strengthen his trust in the midst of difficult times.

For today: when you feel that your problems are bigger than you are, remember that God has acted with power before. Tell Him in prayer what you fear, and trust that He remains faithful.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that the one who spent his time plundering and robbing many nations will end up being plundered by the peoples who remain. The reason is the harm he caused: he shed human blood and destroyed lands, cities, and all their inhabitants. Plundering means taking by force what belongs to someone else.

Habakkuk had asked God why he allowed so much violence and injustice. God answers with a series of warnings against a proud oppressor. It is commonly understood that this refers to Babylon, although the text does not name it here. The message is that God does not overlook injustice, and that violence eventually turns back against the one who practices it.

For today: do not get rich or rise up at the cost of others' suffering. If you see injustice, trust that God is just, and check that your own work and gains are honest.
exp.0:16:
Shall they keep emptying their net and show no mercy as they keep killing nations? Emptying the net means dragging captured peoples out to fish for more. The "net" here is the same thing as a fishing net. Incense is burned as an offering.

Habakkuk speaks with God. The Chaldeans, or Babylonians, are compared to a fisherman who catches nations and even worships his own net, that is, trusts in his own strength. The prophet complains that this violence does not stop. God's answer continues in chapter 2, where he declares that injustice will not last forever.

For today: when you see power being abused and it seems to have no limit, do not keep your pain silent. Bring it honestly to God, as Habakkuk did. And examine your own heart, so that you do not place your trust in your achievements, your money, or your strength, but in God, who is just.
exp.1:11:
God condemns the one who builds up towns and cities through violence, bloodshed and injustice. The word "blood" in the verse refers to murders and crimes. The word "town" means a village or settlement.

The prophet Habakkuk records God's answer concerning Babylon, an empire that conquered peoples and grew rich through plunder. This is one of five "woes," or warnings. The stones and timbers of its buildings would cry out, like witnesses to the injustice. God promises that this violent work will come to nothing, while his glory will fill the earth.

For today: whatever we build, whether a business, a home or a ministry, should be raised with honesty and justice. If something is achieved by taking advantage of others, it will not endure. Let us ask God for wisdom to succeed without harming anyone.
exp.0:0:
It says this book is a "burden," that is, a heavy message from God, which the prophet Habakkuk "did see." By "did see" it refers to his receiving it as a vision or revelation. The word "burden" can also be translated as "oracle" or "prophecy."

Habakkuk is the one speaking, and we know almost nothing else about him; we do not know for certain his family or the exact date when he wrote. The verses that follow show that what weighs on him is his own anguish: he sees violence and injustice all around him and asks God why He does not act.

For today: when you feel the weight of injustice or of God's silence, do not keep it to yourself. Habakkuk brought it to God honestly. Bringing your questions to Him in prayer is an act of faith, not a lack of faith.
exp.0:14:
He says the enemy will catch them all with a hook, trap them in his net, and gather them into his dragnet, which is another old word for a fishing net. Afterward he will rejoice and celebrate his success.

Habakkuk, the prophet, speaks with God and brings him his complaint. He asks why God, being so holy, seems silent while a violent people, whom most readers understand to be the Chaldeans or Babylonians, carries off people as if they were fish. The verses that follow show that this enemy worships his own strength.

For today: if you see injustice and feel that God is silent, you can do as Habakkuk did and bring your questions to him honestly. Praying this way is not a lack of faith; it is trusting that God listens and that he has the final word.
exp.1:8:
This verse is a warning against unjust ambition. To covet is to eagerly desire what does not belong to us. The one who gains dishonest profit for his family and his house seeks to set his nest on high, like a bird that builds up high to be safe. He thinks that this way he will be freed from all danger or misfortune.

God speaks to the prophet Habakkuk, and here announces a "woe" (a sentence of mourning) against the oppressor, which most understand as Babylon. That empire plundered peoples and poured out blood. God says that those who were robbed will rise up, and that the theft will not bring lasting security.

For today: the security built on unjust gain is fragile. Before seeking more, ask yourself whether what you have was obtained honestly. Trust in God as your true refuge, not in what you accumulate.
exp.0:12:
He says that God is so pure and holy that he cannot bear to look at evil or approve of injustice. That is why the prophet asks: if God is like this, why does he seem to keep watching the treacherous and the scornful, and keep silent while the wicked swallows up someone more righteous than himself? The word "wrong" in the verse means harm or injustice.

The one speaking is the prophet Habakkuk, who is talking with God. God has just told him that he will use the Chaldeans (Babylonians), a violent people, to punish Judah. Habakkuk is confused: how can God use a people even more wicked? It is an honest complaint, made with respect and in prayer.

For today: when you do not understand why God allows injustice, do not fall silent or pull away. Bring your questions to him honestly, trusting that he is holy and just, even when his answer takes time.
exp.0:11:
Habakkuk speaks to God and reminds him that he exists from everlasting and is holy. With confidence he says that his people will not be destroyed completely. He affirms that God appointed the Chaldeans (the invading people) to carry out a judgment, and that he established them to correct and punish.

The prophet speaks at the news that Babylon, a cruel and proud empire, is coming against Judah. It mocks kings and worships its own strength. Habakkuk does not understand how a holy God would use a people so wicked. First he leans on what he knows of God, and then he will present his complaint.

For today: when what you see confuses you or hurts you, do not stay alone with what is happening. Remember who God is: eternal, holy, and faithful. You can bring him your questions with honesty and trust that he is still in control.
exp.0:2:
Habakkuk asks God why he is made to see so much wickedness. The old words mean this: "iniquity" is injustice, "grievance" is pain and oppression, "spoiling" is destruction and robbery, and "strife and contention" are constant fighting and conflict. He sees violence all around him and does not understand God's silence.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks, probably in a time of injustice within Judah, though the text does not give the exact date. He is not speaking to the people but to God. His complaint is honest: the law is not respected and the wicked oppress the righteous. God will answer soon, but in a way that will surprise the prophet.

For today: when you see injustice and feel worn down, you can bring your questions to God honestly, as Habakkuk did. Praying this way is not a lack of faith; it is trusting that God listens, even when his answer is late or comes in an unexpected form.
exp.1:2:
This verse says that the vision God gave Habakkuk has not yet been fulfilled, but it has an appointed time. The word that means it will come true and speak the truth is not needed here, so let me put it plainly: the vision will be fulfilled and will not fail. Its promise that it will not fail means it will not fall short. The verse's call to wait with confidence is an invitation to trust, because it will surely come.

Habakkuk, a prophet of Judah, complains to God about the injustice and violence around him. He takes his place like a watchman on the wall to wait for an answer. God speaks to him and tells him to write the vision plainly. The answer announces that God will judge the proud, while the righteous will live by faith. Many understand this as referring to judgment on Babylon, though some also see a broader scope.

When you feel that God is taking his time, do not give up or take shortcuts. Pray, return to his Word, and keep trusting him with patience, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.0:8:
This nation will fall upon its prey, that is, it will come to plunder and to conquer. Its advance is like the scorching east wind, a hot wind from the desert that dries up everything. And it will take so many prisoners that they will be countless, like the sand. Some think the phrase about "their faces" can be translated in other ways, because the Hebrew is difficult.

Habakkuk, a prophet of Judah, complains before God about the violence and injustice among his people. God answers him that He will raise up the Chaldeans, or Babylonians, a strong and cruel empire. Here he describes their power and their eagerness for conquest.

For today: when evil seems to advance without restraint, remember that no human power is eternal or escapes the sight of God. Trust in Him, live justly, and do not put your security in strength or in pride.
exp.1:1:
God answers Habakkuk and tells him to write down what He is about to show him. He is to engrave it clearly on tablets, so that the one who reads it can "run," that is, understand it quickly and carry the message to others, or move ahead without stumbling.

Habakkuk is a prophet who complained to God about the violence and injustice around him. He took his place as a watchman, waiting for an answer. Here God speaks and commissions him to record His reply, which will be fulfilled in its time. Some understand "run" to mean spreading the message; others, reading it quickly and without difficulty.

For today: when you are waiting for answers from God, write down what He shows you in prayer and in His Word. Writing it down helps you remember it, keep your faith while you wait, and share it with others.
exp.1:0:
Habakkuk says he will take his place at his guard post, like a watchman on a tower. There he will stand firm and look carefully from above to see what God will say to him. He will also think about how to answer his complaint or question, which refers to what he had earlier brought against God.

The prophet Habakkuk is speaking. Earlier he asked God why there was so much injustice and violence, and why God would use Babylon to discipline Judah. Now he falls silent and waits for an answer. Some see the image of the watchman as literal, and others as a picture of attentive prayer; the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: when you have hard questions or pain, do not stay stuck in complaint alone. Set aside a quiet moment, open the Bible, pray, and wait with patience. God can speak to you and give you peace, even when the answer takes time.
exp.2:8:
He says God drew out his bow, ready for battle, and that his promises to the tribes of Israel are firm and do not fail. "Selah" seems to be a pause for meditation, though its exact meaning is not certain. Then he says God split the earth with rivers. The bow being uncovered means it was in plain view, with no case over it. "Cleave" means to split or open up.

Habakkuk is the prophet speaking in this verse. He describes God as a mighty warrior who comes to rescue his people, using images of storm and earthquake that recall events from Israel's past. Scholars debate exactly which events the verse refers to. Habakkuk sings this to remember that God keeps what he promises, even when the future looks dark.

For today: when your situation feels uncertain, remember the times God has been faithful, and trust that his word is still secure.
exp.1:10:
What it says: Habakkuk describes something almost unbelievable: the stones of the wall and the wooden beams of a house begin to speak. The "beam of the timber" is the beam or crossbar that holds up the roof. The stones cry out an accusation, and the wood answers as if it agreed.

Context: God himself is answering Habakkuk with a series of woes against an oppressor, probably the Babylonian empire, which grew rich through violence. His house, built with unjust gains, becomes a witness against him. Scholars understand this as poetic imagery, not as a literal event.

For today: What we build through deceit or through harm to others does not stay hidden. Today we can examine how we earn our money and our possessions, and choose honesty even when it costs us more.
exp.2:7:
Here the prophet asks God questions, like someone who beholds something great and is amazed. He asks whether the Lord was displeased with the rivers and the sea when He rode upon His horses and His chariots of salvation, that is, chariots of victory or deliverance.

Habakkuk is the one speaking. He is recalling, in the form of a poem or song, how God acted powerfully in the past, with images of the Exodus and the entry into the promised land. Many understand that the questions do not seek an answer of anger against the water, but show that God governs all creation to save His people.

For today: when your situation feels like a stormy sea, remember that God is greater than that sea. Trust that He knows how to save and to keep His word.
exp.2:3:
It says that God's brilliance was like the light of the sun. Rays of brightness came out of his hand, and right there, within that brightness, his power was hidden. The idea of "rays" can also be understood as "horns" or flashes of light, since the original wording allows both readings. His strength is not fully seen: the light reveals it, but it also covers it.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks in the form of a prayer. He had heard what God would do and was filled with fear. He asks God to act again as he did in the past and, in his anger, not to forget mercy. He remembers when God appeared to his people, in places like Teman and Paran, which are connected with the desert of the exodus, though these details are interpreted in different ways.

For today: when you do not understand what God is doing, remember that his power is real even when you cannot see all of it. Pray with reverence and trust, asking him for mercy and resting in the knowledge that he is still at work.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that the sun and the moon stood still in their place, in their "habitation," that is, in their dwelling in the heavens. Before God, the lights of the sky grow dim: God's arrows (flashes of lightning) and his shining spear (a brilliant lance) outshine them.

Habakkuk is the prophet who prays in the form of a song. He recalls God's mighty works of the past, such as the exodus, and perhaps the time the sun stood still in the days of Joshua (Joshua 10). Some believe this is poetic language and others that it alludes to that event. He sings it to trust in God while he waits for God's judgment on Judah and on Babylon.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, remember who God is. If he rules the sun and the moon, he can care for your life. Pray by remembering what he has done, and trust in him.
exp.0:1:
Habakkuk asks God, "How long?" He feels that he has prayed and cried out for help, but God does not answer. "I cry" means calling out for help loudly. "I call out" is the same, but with more force. "Violence" is wickedness and abuse against others. The phrases "you will not hear" and "you will not save" express what he feels, not necessarily what God does.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks, probably in Judah, before the coming of Babylon, although the exact date is debated. He sees injustice, quarrels, and laws that no longer protect anyone. That is why he complains to God. His book begins with an "oracle," that is, a heavy message from God.

For today: when you feel that God is silent in the face of pain or injustice, do not hide your complaint. Bring it to him honestly, as Habakkuk did, and keep trusting that God hears even when you do not yet see the answer.
exp.2:5:
He stood and measured the earth, meaning he examined it and showed his authority over it. With a single look he made the nations tremble. The ancient mountains and hills, which seem eternal, were broken apart or bowed before him. "Scattered" means broken into pieces; "bowed" means they gave way in surrender. Finally it is affirmed: his ways are everlasting, that is, the way he works does not change or come to an end.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks in a prayer in the form of a song. He remembers how God acted powerfully on behalf of his people in the past, with images of light, trembling and judgment. Many believe it alludes to the exodus and the entry into Canaan, though the text uses poetic language and does not detail every event.

For today: when everything seems unstable, remember that God is firmer than the mountains. Trust that his ways are just and lasting, and rest in him with humility.
exp.1:9:
He says the oppressor planned something shameful to bring honor to his household or dynasty. Instead of protecting it, he destroyed many peoples, and in doing so he harmed himself. "Cutting off" means wiping out or leaving in ruins. "Sinned against thy soul" means that his wickedness turns back against his own life.

Habakkuk records here the words of God, who answers his complaint about injustice. This is the second of the woes against the violent empire, which many understand to be Babylon. The one who grew rich through violence and wanted to secure his place will end up losing everything. God promises that injustice will not have the last word.

For today: do not seek your security or your family's at the cost of others. What is gained through abuse ends up destroying the one who gains it. Trust that God cares for you and act with integrity.
exp.2:18:
God the Lord is the strength of the one who speaks. He will make his feet firm and nimble like those of deer, which leap safely across rocky ground. He will also make him walk on his high places, that is, the mountains or high and difficult places. The last line is a musical note: it is addressed to the choir director, to be played with stringed instruments.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks at the end of his prayer-song. Earlier he saw that a serious crisis was coming: hunger, lost harvests, and empty fields. Even so, he decides to trust and rejoice in God. Some understand the high places as places of safety; others, as victory over difficulties.

For today: when everything seems uncertain, you can ask God for strength for the next step, not for the whole journey. Thank him for what you do have in him, and trust that he will sustain you even on difficult ground.
exp.1:4:
He says the proud man, ruled by wine and by ambition, will not stay at home. His desire is as wide as the grave and as death, which is never full. So he gathers nations to himself and heaps up peoples.

God answers the prophet Habakkuk's complaint about injustice. He promises that his word will be fulfilled, even if it takes time. Then he describes the oppressor, probably Babylon, though the text speaks of him simply as a man. The wine may be literal or figurative, a picture of his drunkenness with power; it is understood in several ways. The verses that follow show that the peoples he has subjected will mock him.

For today: greed never says "enough." You can ask yourself in what area you want more and more, and practice gratitude and generosity. Meanwhile, trust that God is just, and that the righteous person lives by faith.
exp.0:5:
He says that God himself is raising up the Chaldeans, a people who are cruel and swift. They sweep across great territories, not to live in what is their own, but to seize houses and lands that do not belong to them. The word "bitter" here means harsh and fierce, and "hasty" means quick and impetuous. The "dwellingplaces that are not theirs" are the homes of others.

The prophet Habakkuk complains to God because there is injustice and violence in Judah, and the law is not being kept. God answers that he is not silent: he will act, and in a surprising way. He will use Babylon (the Chaldeans) to discipline his people. Scholars point out that this raises a difficult question, which the prophet raises afterward: how God can use a people who are even more wicked.

For today: when it seems that God does nothing in the face of injustice, remember that he still governs, even though his ways may puzzle us. Bring your questions to him honestly, as Habakkuk did, and trust.
exp.1:16:
It says that the violence Babylon did to Lebanon, with its forests and its animals, will fall back on Babylon itself. "Spoil" means violent plundering. "Beasts" are wild animals. "Shatter" here means that it will terrify or destroy. The reason given is the blood that was shed, the seizing of the land, and the harm done to the cities and to those who live in them.

God speaks through the prophet Habakkuk, within a series of woes against the oppressor, which tradition understands to be Babylon. The prophet had asked why God allowed wickedness to prosper. God answers that injustice will not go unjudged. Some explain the mention of Lebanon as a reference to its cut-down forests, others as a general picture of conquest.

For today: God sees the harm done to people and to creation. We can trust his justice and examine whether the way we earn, lead, or use resources respects the lives of others.
exp.2:4:
It says that when God appears, plague or death goes before Him, and burning coals, or hot embers, come out at His feet. Some translate the second part as "fever" or "pestilence"; the Hebrew word has several possible meanings.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks in a sung prayer. He remembers how God acted with His people in the exodus and in their entry into the promised land. He does this to affirm his confidence that God will act again, even though Judah is living through times of injustice and threat.

For today: when evil seems to be winning, remember that God is holy and just, and that He does not ignore injustice. You can pray calmly, handing over to Him what you cannot fix and trusting that He will act in His time.
exp.2:0:
This verse is the title of chapter 3. It says that what follows is a prayer of the prophet Habakkuk. The word "Shigionoth" that appears in the verse is probably a term for a kind of music or song, but its exact meaning is not known with certainty; some think it refers to a style of melody that is lively or emotional.

Habakkuk speaks after having talked with God about the injustice and violence of his time. God announced his judgment to him, and Habakkuk was deeply moved. Now he responds with a prayer that functions as a song, and in it he remembers the mighty works of God in the past.

For today: when you feel confused by what you see around you, turn your questions into prayer. Speak honestly with God, remember what he has done, and trust that he is still at work, even when you do not yet understand everything.
exp.1:12:
It says that God, the Lord of hosts, has determined that everything peoples build with effort but with wickedness will end up burned. Their labors will come to nothing. "Nations" is what the people are, and the phrase about weariness means that they will tire themselves out without achieving anything lasting.

Habakkuk, a prophet, complains to God about the violence and injustice he sees. God answers him with a series of woes against the oppressor, the empire that grows rich through blood and abuse. This verse shows that God sees that injustice and has the final word. Scholars often think of Babylon, though the principle is broader.

Today, before you work hard for an achievement, ask yourself whether you are building it with honesty and justice. What is raised up through deceit or harm to others does not endure; what is done with integrity does have value before God.
exp.1:3:
There are two ways of living. One is that of the proud person, whose soul "is not upright": it is twisted and trusts in itself. The other is that of the righteous, the person who lives well before God, and who "shall live by his faith," meaning they stand firm by trusting and remaining faithful to God. "Lifted up" means being filled with arrogance.

Habakkuk is a prophet who complains because he sees injustice and violence. God answers him and asks him to write down the vision, because judgment on the oppressors will come even though it seems to be delayed. Afterward the proud person is described as someone ambitious who piles up what belongs to others and will end up mocked. Some understand "faith" here also as faithfulness.

When things take a long time or seem unfair, do not lean on your pride or your own plans. Trust in God and remain faithful in the small things of each day.
exp.0:15:
This verse says that the invading people, who catch nations as if they were fish, end up worshiping their own weapons. They offer sacrifices and incense to their net and to their drag, which is another word for a fishing net. The reason is that through them they grew rich: "their portion is fat" and "their meat plenteous" mean that they live in abundance and luxury.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks here, questioning God about why he allows so much violence. The people described are the Chaldeans (Babylonians), according to the context of the book. Some scholars think the sacrifices are literal, and others that it is an image of trusting in one's own strength. Both readings agree on the essentials.

For today: be careful about attributing our success only to our cleverness, money, or work. Let us give thanks to God and use what we have to serve, not to harm others.
exp.2:11:
It says that God, in righteous anger, advanced over the earth like someone stepping forcefully, and that he shook the nations the way grain is threshed. Stepping forcefully is the picture of treading down; threshing is beating the grain to separate it from the chaff. It is poetic language to show God's power in judgment.

Habakkuk, the prophet, prays and recalls how God acted in the past, and he describes God's power with images of creation and of Israel's deliverance. He does this because he sees injustice and fears the invasion that is coming. The following verses explain the purpose: God goes out to save his people and to bring down the pride of the wicked who oppress the poor.

For today: when you see injustice and feel that God is silent, remember that his anger is not capricious; it stands on the side of the weak. You can wait for him with patience, pray with confidence, and in the meantime deal justly and mercifully with those around you.
exp.2:17:
In spite of everything that may be lost, the prophet chooses to rejoice in the Lord. The word "yet" points to "still" or "even so," meaning "despite everything." The Lord is the God of his salvation: he is the one who rescues and sustains him.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks here. He has just heard that a invading nation will come against his people, and the news made him tremble with fear. He pictures a future with no harvest: no figs, no grapes, no olive oil, no flocks or herds, that is, hunger and ruin. Many believe this describes what the invasion would bring. Even so, his trust ends in praise.

For today: when everything goes wrong, your joy does not have to depend on your circumstances. You can weep and be afraid, and still choose to remember who God is and give thanks for what does not change: his love and his salvation.
exp.1:5:
It says that all the peoples who were plundered will raise a mocking song or saying against the oppressor, and they will say, "Woe to him who piles up what is not his!" The word "parable" here means a mocking saying, and "thick clay" is an image of riches taken by violence that become a heavy burden.

God himself answers Habakkuk's complaint about injustice. The prophet has seen a proud conqueror, commonly understood to be Babylon, who grows rich by robbing other nations. This is the beginning of five "woes" that announce that this violence will not go unpunished.

Today we can remember that gaining something unjustly, through deceit, abuse, or imposed debts, does not bring true wealth, but weight. We can honestly examine how we obtain what we have, and trust that God cares for those who suffer injustice.
exp.1:13:
It says that someday the whole earth will be filled with the knowledge of God's glory, in the same way that water completely covers the floor of the sea. That is, there will be no corner where people do not know who God is and how great he is.

"The LORD" is God's name, and "glory" speaks of his greatness and his righteous character.

Here God speaks in response to Habakkuk, a prophet who complained about violence and injustice. God announces woes, or warnings, against the oppressors who build their power with blood and wickedness. Although they may seem to be winning, their work will burn and come to nothing. In the face of that, God promises that in the end his glory will prevail.

For today: when you see injustice and wonder whether everything is lost, remember that God has the final word. Trust in him, practice justice in small things, and share what you know of God with those around you.
exp.1:14:
God condemns the one who makes his neighbors drink, who offers them his poison and gets them drunk in order to see their shame. The first quoted word, "Hiel," refers to something bitter and harmful; the second, "desnudeces," speaks of their shame or humiliation, and perhaps also of their literal nakedness.

Habakkuk records God's answer concerning Babylon, a cruel power. This is the fourth "woe" against it. Some think the image of the wine describes how Babylon subjected and humiliated other peoples; others also see an accusation against its wickedness in general. That is why the following verse says that the cup of God's judgment will come back upon it.

For today: do not use others for your own gain or to mock them. Care for those who are weak, whether through vice, pain, or ignorance. And remember that God sees what is done in secret and defends the humiliated.
exp.2:2:
God comes from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran. These are places in the south, toward the region of Edom and Sinai. "Selah" is a pause for reflection. His glory covered the heavens, and the whole earth was filled with his praise.

Habakkuk, the prophet, prays with fear after hearing what God would do. He asks that God renew his work and remember mercy in the midst of his judgment. To encourage himself, he recalls how God revealed himself to his people in the past. Many believe he is alluding to the Exodus and Sinai, though scholars debate the details.

When everything seems uncertain, pause and remember what God has already done. Looking at his past faithfulness strengthens trust and turns fear into praise.
exp.0:10:
It says that this invading army will sweep forward like a strong wind and move on. But it falls into guilt, because it claims its power comes from its god. The phrase "changes its spirit" can be understood as changing its attitude, becoming filled with pride, or passing on like the wind; translators explain it in different ways. The word "offend" here means that it becomes guilty.

Habakkuk, the prophet, is speaking with God. He complains about the violence and injustice in Judah. God answers that he will raise up the Chaldeans (Babylonians), a cruel people, to discipline Judah. This verse shows that, even though God uses them, they remain responsible for their pride and idolatry.

For today: when things go well for you, do not say that everything happened because of your own strength or intelligence. Give thanks to God and use your achievements with humility. Success does not prove that someone is right.
exp.2:13:
God turned the enemy's own weapons against their leaders. "Pierced" means struck through. Their "staves" are staffs or spears, and "villages" are towns or small settlements. The attackers came like a storm to scatter the people, and their pride made them act like someone who swallows the poor in secret.

Habakkuk prays and sings about what God has done before to save his people. He speaks as a prophet troubled by violence and injustice. Exactly who the enemy is is not made clear here; many think of Babylon, but the passage is poetic and can be applied to more than one oppressor. In the end, the prophet trembles, yet he decides to wait calmly.

When injustice seems to be winning, remember that God sees what is done in secret. You can be honest about your fear, but trust in Him and wait for Him.
exp.1:6:
It says that those who oppress others may be suddenly caught off guard. "Bite" means to attack with cruelty, and "booty" means spoil or plunder. Those who were once victims will rise up, like someone waking from sleep, and will remove the oppressor from his place. He himself will end up being plundered, just as he once plundered others.

Here God speaks, responding to the prophet Habakkuk's complaint about injustice. This passage is the first of five woes against a proud and greedy conqueror. Many understand that it refers to Babylon, although the text does not name it here. The plundered peoples sing a mocking song against him, and God shows that violence does not last forever.

For today: do not envy or imitate someone who gets rich through injustice. Strive to earn and to treat others with honesty, and trust that God sees and corrects what is wrong.
exp.2:16:
Here the verse says that even if the fig tree does not blossom and there is no fruit on the vines, even if the olive crop fails and the fields give no food, and even if there are no sheep in the fold or cattle in the stalls, everything would be lost. The phrase about the olive, which in the source reads as "the labor of the olive fails," means the olive tree disappoints: it does not give the fruit that is expected. The cultivated fields are the land that has been worked, and the food is what sustains people. The fold is the pen where the sheep are kept.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks in a prayer or song. He has just heard how God acts with power and judgment, and his body trembles with fear. He expects an enemy invasion, which would bring hunger and ruin. For this reason he describes a picture of total loss, to show how far he is willing to trust God.

For today: when work, health, or stability is lacking, we can be honest with God about our fear and still choose to trust Him. Faith does not deny the loss; it faces it with hope.
exp.2:1:
He says that Habakkuk has heard what God said and was filled with reverent fear. He asks God to renew his work, that is, to bring it back to life, in the midst of the years, and to make it known in these times. Furthermore, he pleads that even when God acts in anger or judgment, he will not forget his mercy.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks in a prayer meant to be sung, though the exact musical meaning of the term used here is uncertain. Earlier he had received a message of judgment on his people and was frightened. Now, instead of arguing, he recalls God's past works and asks him to act again.

For today: when what is happening around you troubles you, pray with humility and reverence. Ask God to act in your time, and trust that his justice does not set aside his mercy.
exp.1:18:
It is a serious mistake to ask a wooden object to wake up, or a silent stone to rise. An idol cannot teach or guide anyone. On the outside it shines, because it is covered in gold and silver, but on the inside there is no breath at all, no life. The verse's wording about having no breath in the midst of it is the point being made: what looks valuable has no living power.

Here God speaks through the prophet Habakkuk. This is the fifth of several woes against Babylon, a violent and proud empire. God shows that trusting in idols made by human hands is foolish. The verse that follows makes a contrast: the Lord does live and reigns from his holy temple.

Today we might ask where we place our trust: money, success, appearance, or things that shine but cannot give us life. You can bring that trust to God, who does listen, and be silent before him.
exp.0:4:
God invites his people to look at the nations and be amazed. God is going to do something so astonishing, in their own time, that they would not even believe it if someone told them. The phrase "marvel exceedingly" means being so surprised that you are left speechless. "Nations" are the peoples of the world.

Habakkuk, a prophet of Judah, complains to God because he sees injustice, violence, and laws that are not kept. Here God answers. His answer, according to the verses that follow, is that he will raise up the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), a feared people. For Habakkuk it was a puzzling answer, since God would use a harsh nation to act.

For today: when it seems that God is silent in the face of injustice, do not think that he is absent. Keep praying honestly, as Habakkuk did, and trust that God works in ways we may not expect or understand yet.
exp.1:17:
It says that idols are worth nothing. A person carves an image out of wood or stone, or casts it in metal, and then trusts in it. But that image "teaches lies," because it gives a false sense of security, and it is "dumb": it cannot speak, hear, or help. "Carved image" and "molten image" refer to images carved or made from melted metal. "Maker" is the one who fashions them.

God speaks through the prophet Habakkuk. He is announcing woes, or warnings, against a violent oppressor who grew rich through robbery and bloodshed. This is usually understood to be Babylon. God says that his wickedness will come back upon him, and that his idols will not be able to save him.

Today almost no one carves statues, but we can trust in things we have made ourselves: money, success, or prestige. Ask yourself what you rely on when you are afraid. God is alive and hears; trust in Him.
exp.1:19:
This verse says that the Lord is in his holy temple, and that all the earth must keep silent before him. The word "let" is an old-style command, and what it asks for is that the earth stay quiet. "But" introduces a contrast: the idols have no life, but God is present.

Habakkuk is a prophet who spoke with God about the injustice and violence of his time. In this chapter, God answers with a series of woes against the proud and those who trust in idols. Before this verse, God mocks the silent images made by human hands. Scholars debate whether the "temple" is the one in Jerusalem or heaven, and it is possible that it includes both.

Today we can be silent to remember that God is alive and above all things. Before speaking, worrying, or deciding, stop for a few minutes, pray, and trust in him.
exp.0:13:
Here the prophet Habakkuk asks God a question: why do you allow human beings to be treated like fish of the sea or like creeping things, that is, like creatures with no ruler or protector whom anyone can catch? The word "creeping things" here refers to small animals that crawl along the ground, with no one to look after them.

Habakkuk speaks with God because he sees great injustice. The Babylonians, a violent people, were conquering nations. In the verses that follow they are described as fishermen who draw people out with hook and net. The prophet does not understand why God, being holy, seems to be silent.

For today: when you see injustice and feel that God is silent, you can do as Habakkuk did. Bring your questions to him with honesty and respect, and keep trusting that God is holy and just, even though you do not yet understand how he will act.
exp.2:14:
It says God opened a way through the sea for his horses, even though the waters were vast and piled up. "Sea" here is simply the sea, and "heap of great waters" speaks of many stirred-up waters. God's "horses" are a poetic image of his power in action.

Habakkuk, the prophet, is praying with a song. He remembers how God saved his people in the past, and many believe it refers to the Red Sea, although the text uses poetic language and does not name it. Habakkuk recalls this because an invasion is approaching and he is afraid, as the following verses show.

For today: when you face something that seems like a sea impossible to cross, remember what God has already done for his people. That can give you calm to trust Him, even if you do not yet see the way out.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) are a people who cause fear and terror. "Their judgment and their dignity" means that they decide for themselves what is right and consider themselves the highest authority; they recognize no law but their own. "Terrible" means that they inspire great fear.

God speaks, answering the complaint of the prophet Habakkuk, who saw injustice and violence in Judah and asked why God was not acting. God replies that he will raise up Babylon to discipline his people. It is a difficult answer, and the prophet himself questions it later, in chapter 1.

For today: even when human power seems arrogant and unstoppable, it does not have the last word. God still governs history, even when we do not understand his ways. We can bring him our questions honestly, as Habakkuk did, and trust that he is just.
exp.2:9:
It says that, on seeing God, the mountains trembled in fear. The overflowing waters passed by, and the deep ocean lifted its voice, like a roar, and lifted up its hands on high, like one who surrenders or asks for help. The sentence about the old wording is removed, since the words it explains do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Habakkuk, a prophet, prays and remembers how God acted in the past on behalf of his people. Many think he is recalling the Red Sea, the Jordan, and Sinai here, though the text does not say so explicitly. He uses poetic language: all of creation reacts to the presence of the Lord. He does this to strengthen his faith in the midst of difficult times.

For today: when your problems feel like mountains or overflowing waters, remember that all of creation bows before God. Speak to him about what overwhelms you, and trust that he is still greater.
exp.2:15:
When Habakkuk heard what God showed him, his body shook: his belly trembled, his lips quivered, and he felt his bones growing weak, and his legs gave way beneath him. Even so, he says he will wait quietly for the day of distress, when the invading people come.

The prophet Habakkuk is speaking. He had asked God why he allowed injustice, and God announced that Babylon would come as judgment upon Judah. Many understand that here he reacts with fear, seeing God's power and the disaster that is approaching.

For today: you can feel fear and still wait with calm. Habakkuk does not hide his trembling; he brings it to God, and then decides to trust and rejoice in Him.
exp.0:3:
This verse says that the law has lost its force and that justice never truly arrives. The reason is that wicked people surround and press upon the righteous, and so the judgments come out twisted. "Surround" means to encircle or harass; the ungodly person is one who lives without fear of God; "twisted" means unjust or perverted.

The prophet Habakkuk speaks, complaining to God. He sees violence, lawsuits, and corruption among his people, and he asks why God does not act. God will answer that He will raise up the Chaldeans, though the prophet will not understand that plan right away.

Today, if you see injustice, you can speak to God honestly, as Habakkuk did, without hiding your doubts or your pain. And while you wait, you can act with integrity and defend what is right wherever you are, trusting that God sees and has the final word.
exp.1:15:
He says that the oppressor, who thought he would gain glory, has in fact filled himself with shame. Now it is his turn to drink the cup of God's judgment, the cup of the Lord's right hand. "You will be exposed" can be understood as being left uncovered in your shame, although some translations say "show your nakedness" or "stagger." "Vomit of shame" is a strong image of complete humiliation.

God speaks here, answering the prophet Habakkuk's complaint about violence and injustice. This is the fifth of several warnings against a cruel people, probably Babylon, though the text does not name it here. What he did to others now comes back on him.

For today: do not envy the one who prospers by humiliating others. God sees every injustice and does not leave it unanswered. Trust that he will do justice, and seek to treat others with respect and dignity.
exp.0:9:
This verse describes the Chaldeans (the Babylonian army) mocking kings and rulers. No walled city can stop them: "they shall heap dust" means they build earthen ramps against the walls so they can climb up and conquer. To "scoff" is to mock with contempt, and a "strong hold" is a walled city.

Habakkuk is the prophet who speaks. He complains to God about injustice in Judah, and God answers that He will raise up Babylon as an instrument of judgment. Then the prophet is astonished, because God uses a cruel nation to correct His people. The verses that follow say that this power also has limits and will be judged.

For today: even when it seems that the powerful and violence rule without restraint, God remains holy and has the last word. We can bring our questions to Him honestly, as Habakkuk did, and trust that He governs history even when we do not understand how.

sum.2: Habakkuk prays and remembers how God, with glory and power, saved his people and judged the wicked. As he hears it, he trembles with fear. Even so, he asks for mercy and decides to wait patiently. Even if the crops fail and the animals are gone, he will rejoice in God, who is his strength.
sum.1: Habakkuk waits alertly for God's answer, and God tells him to write down the vision: though it may be delayed, it will surely come to pass, and the righteous will live by their faith. Then come five "woes" against the proud and violent man who plunders, sheds blood, and trusts in mute idols. In the end, the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, and the whole earth must be silent before Him.
sum.0: Habakkuk asks God how long He will tolerate violence and injustice among His people. God answers that He will raise up the Chaldeans, a fierce and proud nation that will conquer many lands. Then the prophet, trusting in God's holiness, asks how He can remain silent in the face of such wickedness.
